chunks: "I do it as a floorplan before I route anything, starting from the block diagram. First I list the hard constraints.
Connectors and mounting holes are usually fixed by the enclosure. Antennas want to be at an edge with a keep-out. Hot parts and heat sinks have to be near airflow.
Then I group the circuits by role: power entry and conversion, digital core with its memory and clocks, analog front end, RF, motor or high-current stages, and I/O.
The main rule is to separate the noisy from the sensitive and let the signal flow run through the board in a line.

So power input and big switching stuff go near the power connector, digital sits in the middle, and the analog front end sits in a quiet corner next to its sensor or connector, away from the switching regulator and the clocks.
I put each supply close to the load it feeds, because long power runs mean drop and inductance, and I put decoupling capacitors and crystals right next to the IC they serve.
I keep the ground plane solid and decide where each section's return current flows, rather than cutting it into pieces.
And I check practical things: heat, test points, and whether it can be assembled.
Then I place, look at the ratsnest for tangles, and move blocks until the nets are short and don't cross."
